description: Student of Khwopa College of Engineering, Tribhuvan University, Bhaktapur, Nepal.
summary:
ARES is an interactive 3D Mars exploration and mission-planning platform focused on Jezero Crater and the Martian surface.

The platform brings together NASA and USGS planetary imagery, rover movements, environmental data, spacecraft models and scientific information in one workspace.

It allows users to explore Martian terrain, analyze elevation and potential hazards, plan safer exploration routes, and visualize terrain conditions through elevation profiles.

ARES also features interactive rover, flight and satellite simulations, along with mission reports and data exports.
details:
1. What It Does and How It Works

The application uses CesiumJS to render Mars in 3D. Unlike standard globe applications designed for Earth, it uses the Mars 2000 IAU reference sphere, which has a radius of 3,396,190 metres. This Mars-specific reference system makes it possible to display planetary coordinates, orbital imagery, and rover traverse data accurately.

A Node.js and Express backend manages requests to external scientific data services. It acts as a proxy between the frontend and those services, using in-memory caching to cut down on repeated requests and work around browser CORS restrictions.

The map supports a range of orbital imagery and topographic datasets from NASA Mars Trek WMTS and USGS Astrogeology WMS, including:

- Viking MDIM 2.1

- MOLA Color Relief

- MOLA and HRSC Blended Relief

- MOLA Roughness

- THEMIS Day and Night Infrared imagery

- MRO CTX imagery

- High-resolution HiRISE mosaics of Jezero Crater

Users can switch between map layers, adjust their opacity, and compare datasets in a split-screen view.

The application also presents rover routes and historical mission data from NASA/JPL MMGIS, letting users explore the Perseverance and Curiosity traverses directly on the globe. To bring missions to life, it also includes 3D spacecraft models from NASA’s 3D Resources collection.

Environmental data comes from the MSL REMS and Mars 2020 MEDA instruments. Mars Explorer also brings in NASA DONKI solar storm data, letting users investigate space weather events and their potential effects on Mars. The NASA Image and Video Library helps users find relevant mission imagery and scientific media.

2. Terrain Analysis and Route Planning

Terrain analysis and route planning are among Mars Explorer’s core features.

The application creates an elevation grid for Jezero Crater using Perseverance mission measurements, along with regional MOLA and HiRISE topographic models. This data helps estimate terrain conditions across the map.

Select a location to view its:

- Elevation

- Surface slope

- Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI)

- Distance from known geographical hazards

The analysis accounts for features such as Belva Crater’s walls, Séítah’s sand ripples and the Western Delta escarpment.

Routes are planned using the A* pathfinding algorithm, with costs adjusted for terrain. Users can choose from five planning approaches:

- Low Difficulty

- Avoid Slopes

- Avoid Hazards

- Visit Science

- Shortest Distance

An elevation profile lets users compare routes and see how the terrain rises and falls along each path.

3. Interactive 3D Simulators

Mars Explorer features three interactive simulations that let users explore different aspects of planetary missions.

Flight Simulator

In the flight simulator, users can pilot the Ingenuity Mars Scout or the Ares Supersonic Wing through a 3D Martian landscape. They can explore Jezero Crater, take on navigation challenges or simply fly across the terrain.

Astronaut Rover Simulator

The rover simulator lets users drive either the Ares SEV-6 Pressurized Rover or the Perseverance Utility Chassis across the Martian surface. They can take control themselves or switch on autopilot to follow routes planned by the A* pathfinding system.

While the simulation runs, users can monitor:

- Terrain slope

- Wheel slip

- Battery level

- Oxygen reserves

- Orbiter communication signal strength

Satellite Orbital Transit Simulator

The satellite simulator explores orbital movement and communication coverage. Users can model passes by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey, and Mars Global Surveyor.

The display shows each spacecraft’s orbit, ground-track coverage, solar power, and potential communication relay coverage between spacecraft and the Martian surface.

4. Mission Dossier and Data Export

Users can open a Site Survival Dossier for any selected location to review its geography, terrain conditions, and potential environmental hazards.

Planned exploration routes can also be exported in several formats:

- PDF reports created with jsPDF

- GeoJSON files for external GIS applications

- CSV files with elevation and hazard profile data

5. Benefits

Mars Explorer brings a range of planetary exploration resources together in one workspace. Rather than jumping between NASA imagery archives, rover datasets, weather feeds, and mapping applications, users can access them all through a single interface.

Its terrain analysis tools make geographic information easier to interpret. Users can review elevation, slope, roughness, and nearby hazards before planning a potential exploration route.

The application also clarifies whether information comes from Perseverance mission data, regional topographic estimates, or areas without enough elevation data. This helps users understand the limits of the available datasets.

The export feature also makes it easier to share planned routes and use the generated data with other geographic analysis tools.

6. Intended Impact

The project is designed to support scientific exploration, learning, and the development of mission concepts. Students, researchers, and space enthusiasts can use the application to explore Martian geological features, review past rover movements, and try out different routes across the surface.

It also offers a more accessible way to work with NASA and USGS datasets, which are typically accessed through specialised scientific and geographic software.

By bringing planetary mapping together with interactive simulations, Mars Explorer makes studying the Red Planet more engaging and easier to follow.

7. Tools, Languages and Technologies Used

The application is built with TypeScript, HTML5, and CSS3.

The frontend uses:

- React 19

- Vite

- Tailwind CSS v4

- CesiumJS

- lucide-react

- Motion

- jsPDF

The backend uses:

- Node.js

- Express

- TypeScript

- tsx

- dotenv

External data sources and APIs include:

- NASA Mars Trek WMTS

- NASA Solr Nomenclature Search

- USGS Astrogeology WMS

- NASA/JPL MMGIS

- NASA REMS and MEDA weather feeds

- NASA DONKI Open API

- NASA Image and Video Library API

- NASA 3D Resources repository

The application runs in a standard environment that supports Node.js. On the client side, it works in any modern desktop or mobile browser with WebGL support. A hardware-accelerated GPU is recommended for smoother 3D rendering and simulation performance.

8. Creativity and Innovation

Mars Explorer is designed to be more than a standard planetary map viewer. While many mapping tools focus on showing geographic data, this project links terrain analysis with interactive mission simulations.

For instance, users can plan a rover route with a terrain-aware A* algorithm and then test that same route in the 3D rover simulator. This brings geographic analysis closer to the practical challenges of exploring Mars.

The interface takes inspiration from field manuals. It pairs a full-screen 3D globe with floating panels, navigation controls, and mission details to create the feel of a planetary exploration workstation rather than a conventional dashboard.

9. Factors Considered During Development

Planetary Coordinate Accuracy

To support Martian coordinates and imagery, the default Earth-based WGS84 ellipsoid was replaced with the Mars 2000 IAU reference sphere.

Terrain Safety and Data Quality

Route planning takes slope, terrain roughness, and mapped hazards into account. Warning and danger thresholds can be adjusted; the default slope values are 6° and 15°.

The elevation grid also shows whether data comes from direct mission measurements, regional terrain models, or areas with limited coverage. Routes that extend beyond high-resolution datasets are flagged as provisional.

Reliability and Performance

The backend uses time-to-live caching to avoid repeatedly requesting data from external sources. It also includes request timeouts and fallback options for times when NASA or USGS services are temporarily unavailable.

For example, regional elevation models can be used if high-resolution Perseverance data is unavailable.

User Experience

The interface offers a range of navigation and usability features:

- Camera history controls for revisiting locations you’ve already viewed

- Decimal and DMS coordinate formats

- Signed and 0–360° East longitude conventions

- Keyboard and touch controls for simulators

- Collapsible panels that keep the 3D globe in view as you explore
